units: a neighbour describes an evening spent in a theatre
she sets against each other two venues she attends regularly
in the first venue the scenery is painted onto broad canvases
in the second venue movable panels are shifted in front of the audience
the neighbour prefers the venue that makes her forget she is watching a performance
her brother prefers the venue where the stage machinery is on show
the two of them discuss this question often without ever agreeing
the neighbour ends up granting that each of the two methods calls for a skill of its own
she invites the person she is talking to to come and judge for himself at the next performance
text: My neighbour came back from the theatre the other night and could not stop weighing up the two houses she goes to. At the first, she said, the scenery is painted onto great sweeps of canvas, and the moment the curtain lifts you believe in the old square standing in front of you. At the other, everything hangs on movable panels that the crew shift about in full view, so the audience watches the change happen. She likes the first better, because it lets her forget she is sitting in front of a made-up story. Her brother goes the other way and defends the house where you can see the machinery at work. The two of them turn it over again and again and never agree. In the end she granted that each way asks for a skill of its own. Then she asked me along to the next performance, so that I could settle it myself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: builders of the distant past handed down a set of forms that architects still reuse
the upright support carries the load and divides the space inside
the rounded vault answers the need to roof a wide room with no support in the middle
the curve of that vault carries the thrust outwards to thick walls
the carved band runs beneath the roof
that band turns into pictures the stories the community wished to hand on
the great staircase serves to stage the arrival of the visitor
specialists explain the spread of these forms by the travelling of masters and apprentices
text: Builders of the distant past left behind a stock of forms that architects still reach for. The column heads that inheritance: it takes the weight above, and it breaks up the space inside, giving the eye something to rest against. The dome came out of a plain need, to roof a wide room with nothing standing in the middle; its curve carries the thrust outwards to the heavy walls that ring it. The carved band running under the eaves does other work altogether, setting out in repeated figures the stories a community wanted handed on. Last comes the great staircase, which does far more than lift you a storey: it turns the arrival of a visitor into an event. Scholars who study these buildings put the spread of such features down to the travelling of masters and apprentices from one workshop to the next.

units: the making of a woven hanging runs through several successive stages
a painter first produces a small drawing that settles the colours and the composition
that drawing is then transferred at very large size onto a guide sheet
the sheet is placed behind the threads to steer the hand of the craftsman
the wools are dyed before the weaving
the craftsman records the recipe of each dye bath so the shade can be found again later
the weaving is done on the reverse of the piece
the threads are cut and the edges strengthened when the piece leaves the loom
the workshop discovers the final appearance only after turning the work over
text: A woven hanging never comes into being at a stroke. It begins small, with a painter's drawing that settles the colours and the placing of the figures. That drawing is then blown up to full size on a guide sheet, an enormous thing the weaver hangs behind his threads to steer his hand. The wools go into the dye vats first, and the craftsman writes down the recipe of every bath, so that the same shade can be found again long afterwards. The weaving is worked from the back, which obliges the woman at the loom to picture a face she will not see until the end. Row after row she goes, unhurried, following the outline showing faintly through. When the piece comes off the loom the threads are cut, the edges bound and strengthened, and the work at last turned over. Only then does the workshop see what it has made.

units: a pupil's instrument had lost its biting tone
the maker first ruled out the heavier faults of the instrument
the belly showed no crack and the pegs were holding the tuning
the examination turned next to the bow, whose hair had been drawn too tight
excess tension reduces the contact between the hair and the string
that reduction makes the attack soft and thins the tone in the upper registers
the maker slackened the frog, rubbed the stick down and laid on fresh rosin
the pupil found the tone again from the first notes
the workshop recorded the case because this fault comes back when a quick adjustment replaces a full examination
text: A pupil's instrument had lost its bite, and nobody could say why the tone had gone so dull. The maker she took it to began by ruling out the heavier faults: the belly showed no crack anywhere, and the pegs were holding the tuning without slipping. He turned next to the bow, whose hair had been drawn far too tight after a rehair. Too much tension lifts the hair away from the string, so the attack turns soft and the tone thins out in the upper register. He slackened the frog off, rubbed the stick down lightly and laid on fresh rosin. From the very first notes the pupil knew again the sound that she had thought lost for good. The workshop wrote the case up in its book, since the same fault comes back again and again whenever a hurried adjustment stands in for a proper examination.

units: playing a stubborn piece through in full deepens the difficulty instead of resolving it
the advised method consists in lifting out the passage that causes trouble
the exact bar where the hand falters must be found and marked
the fragment must be played very slowly and with each hand on its own
attention goes to the position of the fingers and not to the page
the speed is raised in successive stages
one must drop back to the previous stage as soon as a mistake appears
the fragment must then be joined to the neighbouring bars because the difficulty often sits in the join
this approach avoids fixing a faulty movement that would have to be unlearnt
text: Playing a stubborn piece through again and again deepens the trouble instead of clearing it. The advised approach is to lift the awkward passage out and treat it as a thing apart. Find the exact bar where the hand falters, and mark it in pencil so that you cannot mistake it later. Then take that fragment very slowly indeed, each hand on its own, watching where the fingers fall rather than following the page. Build the speed up by stages, and drop back to the stage before the moment a mistake appears. Join the fragment afterwards to the bars on either side of it, because the difficulty very often sits in the join itself. The way of working asks for a good deal of patience, but it keeps you from settling a faulty movement into the hand, one that would later have to be taken apart and unlearnt.

units: two neighbouring concert halls have chosen opposite strategies to renew their audience
the first hall has shortened its programmes and done away with the interval in the middle
tickets there cost less and there is no rule about what to wear
the players in that first hall introduce the works themselves from the platform
the second hall has lengthened its break and turned it into a meeting with the audience
listeners in the second hall may come down and question the performers
both managements report attendance on the rise
the first hall draws occasional visitors whereas the second builds up a body of subscribers
a regional study will compare these results at the close of the season
text: Two concert halls in the same town have taken opposite routes to renewing their audience. The first has cut its programmes short and done away with the interval, on the view that newcomers sit badly through an evening broken in two. Tickets there cost less, nobody is told what to wear, and the players introduce the works themselves from the platform. The second hall did the reverse: it stretched the break in the middle and made a meeting of it, with listeners coming down to the front to put questions to the performers. Both managements report attendance on the rise, though the crowds they draw are not the same. The hall with the short evenings pulls in people who come once out of curiosity, while the other is building a body of subscribers. A regional study will compare the two sets of results at the close of the season.

units: an old market hall has been turned into an arts centre
the entrance holds posters and an upright piano open to everyone
the pottery room houses shelves loaded with half-finished bowls
the makers of those bowls come back to finish them in the evening
the dance room has kept its original floor, which creaks underfoot
a narrow room at the far end serves as a recording studio
rugs fixed to the walls there stand in for soundproofing the place could not afford
the upper floor holds a collection of sheet music lent out against a signature
benches have been fitted on the roof to give people somewhere to rest
text: Push open the door of the old market hall that became an arts centre and the first thing you meet is the entrance, cluttered with posters and holding an upright piano that anyone at all may try. On the left the pottery room smells of wet clay, and the shelves sag under half-finished bowls whose makers come back in the evening to finish them off. Opposite, the dance room has kept its original floor, and the wood creaks so loudly that the pupils count their steps by the sound. At the far end a narrow room does duty as a recording studio, with rugs nailed to the walls in place of the soundproofing nobody could ever afford. Upstairs sits the collection of sheet music, lent out against a signature. And on the roof someone has fitted benches, because people needed somewhere to sit between sessions.

units: in the older forms of song the storytelling part was dominant
the repeated part held a brief and secondary role
broadcasting turned that order upside down
a listener paying half attention had to be able to recognise a track very quickly
the repeated part grew longer until it opened the song
listening platforms have sharpened this shift
their payment is triggered after a very short stretch
the writer of the text judges this shift impoverishing
the writer holds that stubborn creators are already showing that the constraint can be escaped
text: Look at how popular song has shifted since its oldest forms. To begin with, the verse carried the story and the chorus was a place to rest: short, almost an afterthought. Broadcasting then turned that order upside down, since a listener paying half attention had to recognise a track within a handful of seconds; the chorus swelled until it opened the song outright. Listening platforms have pushed the same logic further still, because payment is triggered once a very brief stretch has been heard. What we are left with is a craft where the hook comes before all else and the story fades away. You may welcome that and call it a fresh kind of efficiency. I see mainly a loss: a form that gives up on lasting gives up on surprising us too. The most stubborn writers are already showing that the constraint can be escaped.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the workshop calls this specialist the restorer of wall paintings
her mother cleaned the display cases of a regional museum
she went along with her mother when she was a child
that early haunting gave her a taste for damaged surfaces
she studied the chemistry of solvents before she came to drawing
she refuses to act until the origin of the damage has been identified
her colleagues complain about how slow she is
she answers that haste has destroyed more paintings than damp
her methods have been spreading among the younger hands since a whole room was put in her charge
text: In the workshop they call her the restorer of wall paintings, and that title says very little indeed about the doggedness the work demands. As a child she went along with her mother, who cleaned the display cases of a regional museum, and that early haunting gave her a taste for damaged surfaces. Because she could not bear to watch faces vanish under grime, she learnt the chemistry of solvents before she ever learnt to draw. The detour explains her manner: she treats each wall like a patient, and will not touch it until she knows what caused the harm. Colleagues complain that she is slow, and she answers that haste has destroyed more paintings than damp ever did. Since a whole room was put in her charge, her way of working has been spreading among the younger hands of the house.

units: a retrospective given over to the art of glass raises an objection of a technical order
the pieces on show stand on low plinths and are lit from above
this lighting flattens the thicknesses instead of bringing them out
the visitor loses the reading of the inner layers of the objects
the cases have been ranged along the partitions
glass calls for a plain ground and light coming from behind
the reviewer proposes drawing the plinths away from the wall and adding diffusing panels
he also advises bringing down the colour temperature of the sources
he recommends reworking the hang before the announced tour
text: The retrospective given over to the art of glass raises a technical objection that the general reviews have passed over in silence. The pieces stand on low plinths and are lit from above; that raking light flattens the thicknesses instead of bringing them out, and the visitor loses the reading of the inner layers, which is the whole point of such work. The fault lies in the layout: the cases have been ranged along the partitions, when glass asks for a plain ground and for light coming from behind. A remedy exists, and it has been tried elsewhere already. The plinths need only be drawn away from the wall and diffusing panels set behind each object, with the colour temperature of the sources brought down at the same time. The hang deserves reworking before the tour that has been announced.
